name: Japan
summary: Larry finished his service in Japan as a medical-evacuation patient. By his account (August 2026 call), he was flown out of Vietnam seriously ill — likely hepatitis, plus malaria and infections — arriving, as he remembers it, in early September 1965, with the weather turning cold into winter. His DD-214 independently confirms the Japan chapter: his last duty assignment was a U.S. Army medical command at APO SF 96343 (Camp Zama) under U.S. Army Japan. From the hospital he befriended the patient in the bed across from him, a man from back east whose name he no longer remembers; together they explored Tokyo, finding a basement German restaurant called "Heidelberg" off the Ginza. Japan is also where he remembers seeing the Stars and Stripes item reporting him killed in action.
larrysRecollection: Around August 1965, Larry was in Japan. He personally remembers seeing a notice or article in Stars and Stripes saying he had been killed. He went to Japan because he was sick — "sepititis" [as noted; likely hepatitis], malaria, and infections — and lost a bunch of weight; his stool was pure white and his urine looked like Coca-Cola. The weather was cold, going into winter; he placed it as early September. The man in his Japan pictures was in the hospital bed across from him, from someplace back east; they hung out from that day, went to the Ginza strip, found a sign that said "Heidelberg" — a German restaurant downstairs — and ate there.
researchNotes: Research goals: identify the hospital (candidates: U.S. Army Hospital, Camp Zama — APO 96343 — or the 249th General Hospital, Camp Drake); locate the original Stars and Stripes item and any correction, and ask whether he saw it in the hospital ward; find the mid-1960s "Heidelberg" German restaurant near the Ginza in Tokyo directories, servicemen's guidebooks, or Stars and Stripes ads; identify the hospital friend (a fellow patient from back east — likely a different man from the recurring friend in the Vietnam photos); and get the admission and discharge dates from the NPRC file. Captain "Guegler" may be associated with this period. No coordinates recorded until the hospital is identified.
